Behind the scenes of Tuesday’s meeting with Trump, industry leaders questioned the Anthropic boss about his warnings regarding the dangers of artificial intelligence. Congress Wraps Up With a Whimper and a Shrug
 
Plus, why tens of billions of dollars in contested tax bills hinge on two words, and AI CEOs challenged Dario Amodei over his industry warnings
 
 
MARIO TAMA/GETTY IMAGES
 

Good morning. The House and Senate are most likely done legislating until after the midterm elections in November. 

 

There were late attempts to pass a range of bills that would impact everything from college sports to data centers to permitting reform to affordability. But none of the measures will become law anytime soon because Congress has thrown in the towel.

 

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R., La.) has called this Congress one of the most productive of all time. Certainly the One Big Beautiful Bill they passed last year was enormous and consequential, impacting tax policy, immigration policy and government spending.

 

Things gummed up after that. Congress for the most part seized up this year and deferred a lot of authority to the White House on things like war powers and trade. President Trump, with a lot of support from conservatives, pushed Republicans to put everything else on hold unless they could pass changes to election law. That stalled out in the Senate, as did many other things.

 

They did pass a law recently that prevented a government shutdown that would have begun on Thursday, and that’s no small feat in modern Washington.

 

There is deep dissatisfaction with Congress around the country, and dozens of lawmakers are quitting their jobs and not running for re-election. The balance of power has shifted.

 

A new Wall Street Journal poll shows how large numbers of Americans are embracing populist ideas that defy traditional political labels, and this could pose a challenge to the way Congress has worked for many years. The next Congress might have to adapt to these changing political winds, blowing in from the left and the right.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Artificial intelligence: The Federal Trade Commission is investigating Anthropic and OpenAI to determine whether they deceived consumers about artificial intelligence’s potential harms.

 

Trump’s Thursday: The president is scheduled to hold a morning policy meeting and depart for Denton, Texas, where he will deliver remarks at Peterbilt Motors. Later he will travel to Oklahoma and speak at a Republican National Committee midterm rally in Durant, Okla.

 
 
 
CONTENT FROM: ANTHROPIC
 
 
How a Small Lab Is Giving More Patients Next-Day Answers
 
A kidney disease diagnosis is hard enough without a long wait for answers. As case loads grow at Arkana Labs, they’re using Claude to help process referral paperwork with 97–98% accuracy, so patients still get results the day after a biopsy.
 
Learn More  >
 
 
 

What I’m Following

 
 
ALEX BRANDON/ASSOCIATED PRESS
 

Tens of billions in contested tax bills hinge on two words. What does “and continuing” mean? That phrase in President Trump’s 2020 Covid-19 pandemic-disaster declaration is the key to court cases that will determine whether the government turned off tax deadlines for more than three years—and whether U.S. companies and individuals prevail in disputes over billions of dollars.

 

Tech CEOs questioned Dario Amodei for sounding AI alarm bells. Behind the scenes of Tuesday’s meeting with Trump, industry leaders questioned the Anthropic boss about his warnings regarding the dangers of artificial intelligence. Amodei told the other executives that it is important to be honest with the public about model capabilities and not play down risks.

 

Pete Hegseth unveils new command to oversee military-drone technology. The defense secretary is creating a four-star combatant command for autonomous warfare, overhauling how the Pentagon buys, tests and deploys drones and other cutting-edge technologies. In a speech at Marine Corps base, Hegseth said the command is set to be functional in October 2027 and that Elon Musk will help the Pentagon study the future of warfare.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• The Fed watchdog found no evidence of administrative misconduct and no grounds to refer anyone for criminal prosecution over the central bank’s renovations.

 

• Trump began sending $500 checks to nearly one million people with a letter touting his healthcare record.

 

• Senate Republicans made a late push to show voters they were trying to rein in high living costs, but the legislation failed to advance.

 

• Senate Democrats are challenging the legality and prudence of the Pentagon’s plan to take a stake in a Venezuelan oil company.

 

• U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were “strong indications” that Iran played a part in a foiled attack on an air base used by the U.S.

 

• The U.S. pressure campaign leaves Iranian tankers stranded in Asian waters.

 
 
 

What I’m Reading

About Me

 

I’m Damian Paletta, The Wall Street Journal’s Washington coverage chief. I’ve covered Washington for 22 years as a reporter and editor. I’ve covered the White House, Congress, national security, the federal budget, economics and multiple market meltdowns.
